items.title: Burlwood Is Making a Comeback With a Modern Twist
items.summary:
Few materials make a visual statement quite like burlwood. Its swirls and naturally irregular patterns give it a depth and individuality that are difficult to replicate. That distinctive grain comes from burls, rounded growths that develop on tree trunks or branches and are often associated with injury, stress, or infection.

Burlwood gained popularity during the Art Deco era of the 1920s and ’30s before becoming a defining feature of furniture design in the 1970s. Today, it’s experiencing another moment. Yet its current appeal is less about recreating the past and more about rethinking how the material fits modern spaces.

Design Milk spoke with four designers to learn why burlwood continues to resonate and the fresh ways they’re using it.

Bookmatched burlwood creates a striking symmetrical pattern across this three-drawer chest, set against a sculptural curved wood bed frame. Photography by Emily Hart.

Why Burlwood Continues to Captivate Designers 
 “Burlwood does what a great print does,” says Tiffany Brooks , principal designer of Tiffany Brooks Interiors . “It gives your eye somewhere to go. Up close, you see all these little swirls and knots, and from across the room, it reads as one rich surface. Even two pieces made from the same wood can have completely different personalities.”

Abbe Fenimore , owner of Studio Ten 25 , shares that appreciation for burlwood’s organic qualities, seeing the material as a way to introduce visual interest without relying on patterned textiles.

The tightly patterned grain of this burlwood chest extends across its drawer fronts,…
items.t: Burlwood Is Making a Comeback With a Modern Twist

items.title: Adobe's Creative Agent transforms Creative Cloud tools and Firefly workflows
items.summary:
Adobe has rolled out its Creative Agent across the Creative Cloud, providing users with agentic workflows across its platforms to give creatives "more time for their craft".

Unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference in Miami Beach on 10 November, the update spans the brand’s flagship Creative Cloud tools.

The updates were unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference 

Photoshop now features generative restyle and relight, Premiere has a new colour mode, and InDesign now supports co-editing (beta).

Adobe is also bringing the Creative Agent to Firefly – its AI creative studio – through the Firefly AI Assistant, which is currently in beta . 

Users can direct the assistant in plain language, with Adobe stating it has already been used for everything from batch retouching portraits to turning product shots into short-form social videos.

The aim is to help creators take on projects that may previously have required more time, resources or technical complexity. 

Adobe has also launched Firefly Design in beta, a single workspace that combines raster and vector graphics with motion, 3D and print design.

Available as part of Creative Cloud, Firefly Design allows designers to build, review, and hand over projects without leaving the platform.

The conference took place at Miami Beach on 10 November 

Topaz Labs, now part of Adobe, has released two new image-enhancement models, Wonder 4 and Image HDR, which are sold separately through Topaz.

Adobe said the Creative Cloud updates respond to the way creatives are increasingly working – juggling more formats, apps and mediums while being…
items.t: Adobe's Creative Agent transforms Creative Cloud tools and Firefly workflows

items.summary:
A large light well brings daylight deep into this private home that was designed by Desai Chia Architecture for a tight site in a dense Maryland neighbourhood.

The project takes its name from its location in Bethesda, a city located northwest of Washington DC.

The house is set within a suburban neighbourhood near the downtown district, where residential lots are about one-fifth of an acre (647 square metres). Because the houses here are close together, the architects needed to be very mindful of privacy concerns.

“The clients sought a house that would feel open and light-filled without sacrificing privacy,” said New York-based Desai Chia Architecture .

“Its compact lot and the close proximity of neighbouring houses required a careful response balancing both openness and discretion."

The architects intended the house to “rethink suburban-urban hybrid living through a modern lens”.

Roughly rectangular in plan, it has three levels and a basement. Setbacks help break up the mass, particularly on the street-facing elevation.

items.title: David Rockwell Takes Us Inside the Design of Skywalker Grill
items.summary:
Designing a restaurant for George Lucas might seem like an invitation to draw from the filmmaker’s extensive cinematic universe. But when David Rockwell and his team began developing Skywalker Grill , the signature restaurant at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, the conversation went in a different direction.

Rather than referencing the Star Wars franchise or any of Lucas’s other films, the restaurant would take its cues from something more personal: Skywalker Ranch , the filmmaker’s creative retreat in Northern California. Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, envisioned a space that felt warm, intimate, and welcoming, a deliberate contrast to the futuristic architecture of the museum designed by Ma Yansong of MAD Architects .

Photography by Tom McGovern

In the latest episode of Once Upon a Project , Rockwell joins host AJ Paron to discuss how that vision took shape, from the unconventional fabrication techniques behind the restaurant’s sculptural wood interior to the decisions that shaped its relationship with the surrounding museum.

“They wanted to start the conversation around warmth and the kind of warmth of Skywalker Ranch in many facets, not only material palette but also custom furniture,” Rockwell explains.

Photography by Tom McGovern

That direction ultimately led to an interior defined by rich cherry wood, curved banquettes, custom furnishings, and carefully integrated lighting. One of its most striking features is a continuous wood shell that wraps from ceiling to walls, creating an almost cocoon-like environment. According to Rockwell, there…
items.t: David Rockwell Takes Us Inside the Design of Skywalker Grill

items.title: Meet Laerke Ryom, Patricia Urquiola's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years
items.summary:
Architect and designer Patricia Urquiola has chosen fellow multidisciplinary Laerke Ryom as her pick for Dezeen’s 20x20 project, in partnership with Kohler . In this interview , Ryom discusses her innovative work and how it's rooted in Danish design traditions.

Ryom, who is based in Copenhagen, first came to many people's attention as one of the co-founders of the design community Ukurant .

Above: Laerke Ryom, photographed by Alexander Höllsberg for Innenkreis . Top image: her work includes pieces made from wood offcuts. Photo by Heidi Lerkenfelt 

Together with fellow founders Josefine Krabbe Munck , Kamma Rosa Schytte and Kasper Kyster , Ryom showed her work as part of its first exhibition at Danish design week 3 Days of Design in 2020 , and Ukurant quickly became a recurring highlight of the design event.

Patricia Urquiola selected Laerke Ryom for Dezeen’s 20×20 project. Photo by Nicola Carignani 

Since graduating from the Royal Academy of Fine Art in Copenhagen's master’s program in furniture and object in 2022, Ryom's tactile designs have continued to evolve, and she has worked with a range of materials and products.

For her collection Blå, she made handwoven denim upholstery out of worn-out jeans, while the Buckle chair , made with furniture brand Fredericia, resembles a leather jacket.

"I find very interesting the way she moves naturally between furniture and textiles, starting from discarded materials and giving them a new logic through simple gestures," Urquiola said of why she chose Ryom.

"There is something light in the way she works. Her work feels open…

items.title: Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging designer of the year Simon Skinner
items.summary:
This year Simon Skinner was named emerging designer of the year at the Dezeen Awards . Here, he selects five projects that showcase his work.

Swedish designer Skinner set up his studio in 2020 and has rapidly become known for his sculptural furniture and installations that explore rethinking and reusing found materials.

"My practice is centred around material culture, exploring the relationship between objects, meaning and everyday life," Skinner told Dezeen.

"What connects my work is an interest in how forms carry associations and how these can be reshaped to offer new perspectives on things we know and take for granted."

Skinner finds that the things that excite him about design are also "the same things that make me suffer".

"You never quite know what’s coming next when running your own practice, but there’s also something exciting about that uncertainty," he said.

"A material or an object you’ve overlooked for years can suddenly become the starting point for a whole body of work."

Over the coming year, along with creating new collections and public installations, Skinner hopes to dedicate more time to research.

"I want to make more room for research and experimentation, and give myself time to follow an interest before knowing exactly where it might lead," he said.

"When I started researching Afro combs at Konstfack , I became aware of how much history and symbolism an everyday tool can hold. That experience still informs how I work," he continued.

"I want to keep exploring the objects and forms we take for granted, looking at the meanings they’ve inherited…
items.t: Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging designer of the year Simon Skinner

items.title: Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?
items.summary:
For more than a decade, buildings bearing trees have been sprouting up all over the world, from New York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney. 

It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including BIG , MVRDV , MAD and Ateliers Jean Nouvel .

And yet, not everyone is a fan. Almost every time Dezeen publishes an arboreal structure, a volley of comments crying greenwashing and gimmickry soon follows.

So, are the haters right on this one? Or do the arguments stack up in favour of wooded buildings?

The root of the issue 

To proponents of the approach, some of the benefits of putting trees on buildings are indisputable.

"I'm totally in favor of not only trees on buildings, but any type of natural habitats on buildings wherever it's possible," said Fernando Scherner, an associate director in the nature and biodiversity team at engineering firm Buro Happold . "There are a few things that I think we can't even argue about anymore."

There is, Scherner told Dezeen, strong evidence that vegetation on buildings bolsters biodiversity . And, he says, "there's no discussion" that done right, shade and evapotranspiration from leaves can effectively keep homes cooler in hot weather, reducing the need for air conditioning – and therefore energy use.

But this second point gestures towards the crux of the debate about trees on buildings.

Tree-planted terraces wind around BIG's The Spiral skyscraper in New York City. Photo by Laurian Ghinitoiu 

Such buildings require extra structural material to support the weight of…
items.t: Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?

items.title: Staff at Edinburgh College of Art criticise "financially-driven" closure of design courses
items.summary:
Over one hundred staff at Edinburgh College of Art have signed an open letter addressed to the university, calling on the institution to reverse its decision to cut three craft -focussed design courses from its programme.

Open letter states "deep concern" 

The open letter was signed by 109 unnamed staff members of Edinburgh College of Art , which announced on 15 September that it would stop admitting students for its undergraduate courses in jewellery and silversmithing, textiles and performance costume from 2027.

The move is part of a wider decision by the University of Edinburgh , which the art college merged with in 2011, to make £140 million's worth of cuts to arts and humanities courses. 

"We the undersigned are writing to mark our deep concern about the University of Edinburgh's current financially-driven restructuring," states the letter, which was written by an unnamed senior lecturer in the school of design and published yesterday. 

"As staff who collectively provide and deliver the teaching, research, technical expertise and administration of design, we assert that there is irreparable harm being done to the core values of our subject area, school, and to the art, craft and design professions in Scotland at large," it continues.

The open letter also asks the university to retract its decision to close the courses and requests better communication between the university and its employees.

items.title: Assemble covers miniature agricultural buildings in intense blue pigment for Building Blue exhibition in Tokyo
items.summary:
Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that "play with scale" to showcase a new pigment, made from industrial waste by design studio Matter at hand, at Tokyo 's SKAC gallery.

With the exhibition, the UK-based collective said it aimed to "explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour".

Photographs 

Previous 

Next 

Photographs

Close 

The exhibition was jointly created by the two studios to showcase the new pigment, developed by Matter at hand from local waste material, on the miniature buildings made by Assemble .

The blue hue was manufactured by Japanese company Nikken to be used in the Play Earth Park – a campsite designed by Assemble that is currently under development in rural Japan.

"The pigment was essentially created by analysing local material waste streams in Toyama and exploring what kind of different colours could be produced from them," Matter at hand founder Lewis Jones told Dezeen.

"In the end, the blue uses a combination of rice husk ash, limestone filter dust, recycled glass and copper, which are mixed together with water to form a thick clay-like paste and then heated in an electric kiln to around 950ºC," he continued.

"The materials react to form a new crystal phase – known as cuprorivaite, which is bright blue."

To show it off, Assemble constructed three miniature houses from Japanese cedar that draw on the agricultural buildings found close to where the pigment material was sourced. The houses were named The Hut, The Tower and The Bird.

items.title: Thermory Design Awards 2026 recognises striking examples of architecture and design using thermowood
items.summary:
A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood .

Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.

The dramatic roof form of Under the Reed Roof, winner of the interior category, defines both its exterior and interior. Photo by Mykhailo Lukashuk 

Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals. 

The treatment enhances the material’s dimensional stability and reduces moisture uptake compared with untreated wood, according to Thermory .

Thermory thermowood has a wide variety of possible uses. Photo by Mykhailo Lukashuk 

The winner of the interior category is a trio of Ukrainian guesthouses collectively named Under the Reed Roof, designed by Kyiv-based studio YOD Group .

Each guesthouse comprises a glass-walled volume at the base, topped by a tapered thatched roof with exaggerated proportions.

Thermo-ash shingles feature in the interiors. Photo by Mykhailo Lukashuk 

While the exterior of these roofs is made with traditional reeds, the interiors are lined with thermo-ash shingles, arranged to create a tactile effect that is repeated on the front doors.

These highlight the interplay between the interior's traditional and contemporary design elements, contrasting materials, and…

items.title: The Volvo EX60 Draws on Forest Walks and Nordic Seas
items.summary:
“Scandinavian design never shouts, but when you come closer, you are rewarded,” says Sara Erichsen Susnjar, senior color and material design manager at Volvo Cars . Detail by detail, the automaker’s new all-electric EX60 bears this out. Its seats carry a pattern drawn from two seas converging off the coast of Skagen, Denmark; its base carpet borrows its hue from foraged finds from the woods outside the company’s studio in Sweden; and an interior lighting option fills the cabin with the silhouettes of leaves.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars

Erichsen Susnjar, who has spent 20 years at Volvo Cars, oversaw color and materials for both the EX60 and the EX60 Cross Country. Under her direction, the team looked to the natural world for the car’s colors, patterns, and textures, often starting with what turned up on a walk.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars

Forest Finds 
 Gathering began close to home, on outings that were already part of the team’s routine. “We are very fortunate to have the forest just outside our design studio, so it naturally becomes part of our everyday life, whether we go there for lunch, a coffee break, or simply to clear our minds,” Erichsen Susnjar says.

Photography courtesy of Volvo Cars

Over time, the team began bringing small pieces of the landscape back inside: mushrooms, twigs, stones, moss, and herbs. Each was studied for its pattern, color, and texture, then cast or digitized, and the findings became prompts for new ideas. Traces of the work appear in subtle patterns on the seatbacks and door panels, as well as in the shade of the base…
items.t: The Volvo EX60 Draws on Forest Walks and Nordic Seas

items.title: Dezeen reports from New York's new November design week
items.summary:
A collection of showcases, old and new, took place in New York this November, effectively adding a second design week to a city already loaded with events. Dezeen's US editor Ben Dreith explores the offerings.

The as-yet-unofficial design week in the first weeks of November came into focus earlier this year, when trade fair ICFF, anchor fair of NYCxDesign , announced that in 2027 it will take place simultaneously with sister fair BDNY, which has been held in November for years.

The move has prompted questions in the city about the future of the NYCxDesign festival in May and what a November design week would look like.

Dudd Haus at Collectible design fair was a standout booth from the week. Photo by Matthew Gordon 

While BDNY and high-end showcase Salon Art + Design have always been held in November, other design fairs have sprouted to take advantage of the opportunity to show during this busy period.

The week is positioning itself, without any explicit organisation, as a massive event in the New York design calendar. 

Even NYCxDesign, still scheduled for May as usual in 2027, held a November event bringing in designers Ross Lovegrove , Karim Rashid and Rem D Koolhaas for a talk moderated by New York-based design writer Camille Okhio . 

The panellists spoke about the potential for AI and derided the inclusion of craft in conversations about design. However, as writer Debika Ray noted in an opinion piece for Dezeen, crafted, one-off pieces have lately come to dominate design shows . 

NYCxDesign staking out a talk with well-known industrial designers suggests that…
items.t: Dezeen reports from New York's new November design week

items.title: ‘The Terence Conran of his day’: the visionary Victorian futurist adored by design superstars today
items.summary:
A professor at the age of 21, Christopher Dresser was a design genius who created beautiful, futuristic homeware, from teapots to toast racks to jugs. Why is his brilliance only now being recognised?

Victorian industrial designer Christopher Dresser was always a visionary. As a child, he was so artistically gifted he went to design school in 1847 when he was just 13. He became a professor at 21, dreaming up theories based on plant structure that changed the way designers worked.

But it was after he quit academia that he really started to break boundaries. As a self-declared “design doctor”, he experimented with production techniques that brought beautiful, futuristic homeware into everyday houses. He was one of the first western designers to travel to Japan, helping introduce Japonisme to British life, which has had a transformative effect on furniture and decoration ever since.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘The Terence Conran of his day’: the visionary Victorian futurist adored by design superstars today

items.title: Davis Furniture and jehs+laub Introduce the Sculptural Laken Nesting Tables
items.summary:
Three steel parts shape the silhouette of the Laken Occasional Table Series : a spun cone settling low against the floor, a slender column drawing upward from its center, and a second cone opening wide to cradle a circular top. The dual-cone composition gives jehs+laub ’s design for Davis Furniture its distinctly modern profile, extended to a set of three nesting tables.

Designed to nest seamlessly or stand alone, the three round tables scale from a single grouping to individual pieces. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

Laken continues a collaboration between Davis and jehs+laub that began in 2009, and it carries forward the studio’s approach to balancing soft curvature with precise, architectural form. On every Laken table, gentle radii and careful proportions ease the move from flared base to slender column to inverted cone, and each piece appears fully resolved from any angle.

Nested together or used on their own, the tables can be layered into a single, dynamic arrangement or spread throughout an interior, adapting to lounge, hospitality, and collaborative environments.

Each round tabletop is supported by an inverted steel cone. Image courtesy of Davis Furniture.

The sculptural form belies a carefully engineered base. Its spun steel cones and steel column are mechanically fastened through concealed hardware for a tight, durable assembly built to perform over time, and a ballast hidden within the lower cone brings the center of gravity down, giving the tables stability and resistance to tipping.

items.title: "Intensely physical patterns" cloak Gerhard Richter's self-designed gallery in Doha
items.summary:
Kaleidoscopic patterns adorn the exterior of this pavilion in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio Selldorf Architects as an art gallery. 

Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei .

It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter's own work.

Richter designed the Doha Pavilion with Selldorf Architects as a reference to his Strip paintings – a series that involved digitally dividing his Abstract Painting artwork into vertical stripes, building on his earlier explorations of colour, pattern and repetition.

"My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work," said Richter.

"The pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the patterns that first led me to the Strips," he continued. "Doha is the right place and the only place for my pavilion.”

Doha Pavilion has a six-sided form, wrapped in psychedelic tiles displaying repeating, kaleidoscopic patterns that recall geometries seen in Islamic art, nodding to the project's context.

Selldorf Architects founder Annabelle Selldorf said the design reflects a "profound culmination of many years of [Richter's] research into abstraction".

items.title: Meet Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Lesley Lokko's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years
items.summary:
Ghanaian-Scottish architect Lesley Lokko has nominated Courage Dzidula Kpodo as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler .

In this interview he explains why despite growing global attention, his ambitions remain resolutely local.

Having only graduated in 2025 from a master’s in architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) – for which he was awarded the Arthur Rotch Prize for highest overall mark – Kpodo is already someone Lokko believes will "help shape the next chapter of African architecture".

Kpodo’s work, which sees him blur the roles of architect, artist and archivist, is focused on revealing what he calls the “silences” in prevailing narratives about Ghanaian architecture, and challenging the idea that Ghana’s future development must be a "linear prescription of urbanisation".

If this sounds theoretical or speculative, Kpodo’s approach is anything but: the site of his MIT thesis was an almost five-acre stretch of farmland in Ghana to which he purchased a 99-year lease in 2022, and is currently using as a live site to consider alternative forms of development in the region.

Lesley Lokko (above) has selected Courage Dzidula Kpodo for Dezeen's 20x20 project. Photo by Festus Jackson Davis. 

Stating how, if nothing else, the purchase would "preserve the value of the money I had in my savings account," Kpodo sees the site becoming an alternative institution of sorts, constructed using materials he has salvaged from vernacular buildings that would otherwise be demolished.

items.title: Biscuit-tin lids, horse brasses and scrap metal form sculptural V&A Christmas tree by Burberry
items.summary:
Fashion brand Burberry 's chief creative officer Daniel Lee worked with artist Ann Carrington to create a Christmas tree sculpture for the Victoria & Albert Museum , made from "memories, traditions and little treasures."

The 16-foot (4.8-metre) tree, which was unveiled this week, sits in the entrance hall of the Victoria & Albert Museum (VA's) South Kensington location and was designed to celebrate craft and creativity.

"This collaboration with Ann is a celebration of creativity and what better place to showcase this than the V&A?" Lee said. "It’s one of my favourite museums and a constant source of inspiration to me."

Lee and Carrington made the tree from old money boxes, biscuit and sweet-tin lids, trinket dishes, silver trays, horse brasses and embossed plates, which were turned into rosettes and ribbons and attached to a metal frame.

The tree, which was made as part of Burberry 's 170th anniversary celebrations, also features ribbons and bows made of scrap metal.

According to Lee, he and Carrington made the sculpture from "memories, traditions and little treasures. Objects and materials that most people would overlook."

Read:

Burberry unveils "archive-inspired" charging knight logo 

Carrington added that the design was inspired by the ritual of getting old Christmas decorations out of storage in time for the festive season.

"We wanted to capture that magical moment when you retrieve the battered old box of Christmas decorations from the loft, sift through the faded party bows and tattered tinsel accumulated through the generations and begin the joyful ritual…

In the 70s and 80s Essex of my youth, no one had a real Christmas tree unless they lived in the country, or perhaps Loughton. Our family’s skinny artificial tree is now 55 years old and comes out every year at my sister’s. It’s shed a few plastic “needles” down the years, but it’s still standing proud – which is more than you can say for a real Christmas tree bought in 1971, or even 2025.

Therein lies the surprising environmental efficiency of artificial Christmas trees. The Carbon Trust says using a fake tree over seven to 20 years (depending on its weight and materials) can create fewer emissions than buying a new, commercially grown tree every year. The key is to buy an artificial tree you’ll love enough to roll out for decades.

items.title: Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging architect of the year Kuma&Elsa
items.summary:
This year Kuma&Elsa was named emerging architect of the year at the Dezeen Awards . Here, they select five projects that demonstrate the ethos of the studio.

Led by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French-Spanish urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa has completed a wide variety of projects from their bases in France and Japan.

"We believe it is important not to impose a common consistency across our projects," Kuma told Dezeen. 

"Every project is unique, shaped by a one-off combination of site and client. Preserving that uniqueness requires an open mind. Personally, I quickly lose interest when things are planned in advance."

"That said, there are certain topics, many of which are shared by our generation, such as feminism, the care for natural resources and a shared public space, that interest us on a personal level, and I imagine they find their way into our work," added Escobedo. 

Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo lead Dezeen Award-winning studio Kuma&Elsa 

"We try to approach them with a sense of joy."

Although they have already designed a wide range of projects, from installations to houses and public toilets, the duo would like to work on more varied schemes and unusual projects, along with completing their own, long-running renovation.

"It would be nice to actually finish this self-renovation project at some point..." said Escobedo. 

"More seriously, I'd love to experiment with the reuse of materials on a larger scale, or in a European context, working with European craftspeople."

"I would love to work on overlooked building types and uses, especially…

Architecture studios Stanton Williams , Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have completed their long-awaited transformation of the 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum.

Opening to the public on Saturday, the former Victorian market hall now functions as a museum that tells the story of London's history through exhibitions designed by German studio Atelier Brückner .

According to the London Museum , it is the largest dedicated city museum in the world.

The London Museum is opening this weekend

Ten years in the making, the opening of Smithfield General Market marks the first phase of the London Museum's relocation from the Barbican Estate's former Museum of London, which is set to be demolished .

Stanton Williams , Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have overhauled the General Market, which fell into disrepair after it closed in the 1990s, and will also convert the adjacent 1960s Poultry Market , which is expected to open in 2028.

Spanish studio Raúl Sánchez Architects turned a former washhouse into Casa de las Lavanderas, with a lightwell that is a "modern translation of the old wells" used by local laundry workers.

The home is located on Barcelona's picturesque Calle Aiguafreda street, historically an area where washerwomen used wells to handwash their clients' clothes.

The lower level of the 80-square-metre building was partly underground and very dark, leading the studio to look for new solutions to add more light.

"Since the ground floor is semi-basement, the area furthest from Aiguafreda Street was darker, so to bring light into it, I incorporated this lightwell topped with a skylight," studio founder Rául Sánchez told Dezeen.

The lightwell also functions as a "modern translation of the old wells" that used to provide water for the laundry workers.

Architecture practice New-works adapted the building for hospitality use, establishing a series of communal spaces at ground level that could serve as a social hub for guests.

items.summary:
Plaids and florals might seem more at home on upholstery or wallpaper than ceramic tile, but Fireclay Tile’s latest collection makes a compelling case for bringing those familiar patterns to harder surfaces. Called Idyllwild, the new hand-painted collection takes inspiration from traditional textiles, translating everything from delicate botanical illustrations to richly layered plaids into ceramic designs that feel both nostalgic and contemporary.

Interestingly, the collection didn’t begin with flowers at all. “We were seeing designers use a lot of intricate textiles, colors, and patterns together,” explains Jamie Chappell, VP of Brand and Product at Fireclay Tile, adding that early explorations focused on plaids and stripes. “As a true lover of ’90s alt-rock, I actually went down a rabbit hole early on, wondering if it should be a ‘grunge’ collection.”

Fireclay Tile’s Idyllwild collection in its Winter palette, featuring deep blues, earthy greens, and warm neutrals across floral, striped, and plaid patterns.

That direction eventually gave way to something softer. Recognizing the longstanding relationship between florals and plaids in interiors, the team introduced botanical patterns to balance the collection’s more structured designs. The name Idyllwild followed, referencing the California mountain town.

The resulting collection includes 16 patterns organized into four categories: Specimen Flowers, Idyllwild Florals, Idyllwild Stripes, and Idyllwild Plaids.

items.title: Art Meets the Slopes at Powder Mountain’s Outdoor Gallery
items.summary:
Most skiers and snowboarders will likely pause at some point during a day on the slopes to take in their surroundings. After all, ski resorts typically offer great mountain views. But at Powder Mountain in Utah, visitors get more than a scenic view. They might also encounter a bright pink pineapple rising among the pines, a classical Greek column twisted into an improbable shape, or poetry carved into a boulder. These three installations are the latest additions to Powder Art Foundation ’s skiable outdoor art museum, an evolving collection that challenges how—and where—we experience art.

Davina Semo’s Listener (2020–2024), a patinated cast-bronze bell, is part of Powder Art Foundation’s outdoor art collection at Utah’s Powder Mountain. Photography courtesy of Powder Art Foundation.

Established in 2024 in partnership with Dia Art Foundation , Powder Art Foundation occupies 8,000 acres of Utah’s Wasatch Mountains. The foundation’s goal is to bring contemporary installations into dialogue with the landscape while honoring the region’s connection to the Land Art movement.

“We’re building a collection that people encounter while spending time outdoors, so I’m interested in work that can surprise you and hold your attention without needing a museum around it,” says Alex Zhang, chief creative officer of Powder Mountain.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home's original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G , was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

items.title: Meet AMAA, Neri&Hu’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years
items.summary:
An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen's 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler .

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio , a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

"AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse," said the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures "positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture".

items.title: RIBA president rejoins ARB register to restore architect title
items.summary:
The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects , Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board , nearly a year after terminating it. 

In a LinkedIn post , Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board's (ARB) register because he no longer wanted "to face the prospect of legal action".

Specifically, he said he feared the potential "legal proceedings and financial penalties" from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

"I have felt the fear of legal proceedings" 

Williamson's post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework” . 

This ARB framework currently only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a new regulatory model for UK architects.

Read:

RIBA president Chris Williamson to give up architect title 

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson said his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

"Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register," he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

items.t: RIBA president rejoins ARB register to restore architect title

“I think a big part of the intention is that he takes home with him wherever he goes; conceptually, the idea was to take ‘the ville’ to the world,” he continued.

“And what better way to do that than something that lives basically at the centre point of the entire city?”

Other nods to the rapper’s life in Fayetteville include the presence of a Honda Civic car, which Martinez describes as a “supporting actor in the show”. 

Positioned in front of the building at centre stage, the car is supported on ties that allow it to be suspended above the stage during specific moments of the performance.

items.title: ‘The platonic ideal of a wine glass’: we test the best for every budget
items.summary:
Searching for a wine glass that can do it all? From short-stemmed to swirlable, dishwasher-friendly to delicate, here’s the glassware that’s a cut above the rest

• The best no- and low-alcohol wines for when you’re off the booze

It is a truth only sometimes acknowledged that wine is in want of a good drinking vessel. Why? Because wine experts agree that the shape, character and feel of a glass give wine the conditions to shine.

“A good glass can greatly improve your experience,” writes David Williams in The Encyclopedia of Wine. He adds that expense isn’t necessary: “[A]s a rule, the thinner the glass the better, while an oval shape and generous (but not enormous) bowl are best at capturing and releasing a wine’s flavours.” Drinking wine is an experience beyond flavour; before the taste, there is the nose, and a good glass will amplify its aromas. Likewise, there is the ineffable question of how a wine makes us feel; again, your choice of glass feeds into this experience – how does it feel to hold, to swirl, to sip from?

Continue reading...
